source: built-in example (proportion-ma/index.html #src), default options: logit transformation, Paule-Mandel tau2
plain: This analysis combined 7 studies with 1,040 participants in total. Across these studies, the average proportion of participants with the outcome was estimated at 8.5%. Allowing for chance, the true average is likely to be in the range 6.9% to 10.3% (95% confidence interval). The amount of variation between the studies’ results beyond what chance would explain might not be important (I² = 0.0%). In a new setting similar to these studies, the proportion could plausibly be anywhere from 6.6% to 10.8%. This summary describes how common the outcome was in the included studies; it does not show why the outcome occurs or how much it matters to patients.
methods: Proportions (events divided by participants in each study) were pooled with an inverse-variance random-effects model; the between-study variance (τ²) was estimated with the Paule–Mandel method (Paule and Mandel 1982). Analyses used the logit transformation (log odds of the proportion) with within-study variances computed from the event and non-event counts. For studies with no events or with all participants having the event, 0.5 was added to both the event and the non-event counts (boundary-only continuity correction; Sweeting et al. 2004); no correction was applied to any other study; no included study needed this correction. The pooled estimate and its limits were back-transformed with the inverse logit. The 95% confidence interval (CI) for the pooled estimate used a normal (Wald) approximation on the analysis scale, without the Hartung–Knapp adjustment. Study-level 95% CIs are exact Clopper–Pearson intervals (Clopper and Pearson 1934). Heterogeneity was summarised with Cochran’s Q, τ² and I², where I² was computed from Q as (Q − df)/Q, expressed as a percentage and truncated at zero (Higgins and Thompson 2002); with the Paule–Mandel estimator this Q-based I² can differ from the τ²-based I² reported by some software. I² was interpreted with the overlapping bands given in Cochrane Handbook v6.5, §10.10.2. A 95% prediction interval was computed on the analysis scale as the pooled estimate ± t × √(τ² + SE²), with t from a t distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of studies minus one (Cochrane Handbook v6.5, §10.10.4.3; Higgins, Thompson and Spiegelhalter 2009), back-transformed in the same way, and reported when at least 3 studies were available. Analyses were run in allmeta proportion-ma <build.version> (commit <build.shortSha>).
results: The analysis included 7 studies with 1,040 participants and 88 events. The pooled proportion was 8.5% (95% CI 6.9% to 10.3%) from a random-effects model (Paule–Mandel τ²) on the logit scale. Between-study variance τ² = 0.0000; Q = 0.23 (df = 6); I² = 0.0% (Cochrane Handbook v6.5, §10.10.2: might not be important). The 95% prediction interval for the proportion in a new study similar to those included was 6.6% to 10.8%.
flags: Fewer than 10 studies: tests for small-study effects (funnel plot asymmetry) would be underpowered, and none were performed.
An I² of 0.0% does not show that the studies are homogeneous; with few studies, heterogeneity statistics have low power.
references: Paule RC, Mandel J. Consensus values and weighting factors. J Res Natl Bur Stand 1982;87:377-385.
Sweeting MJ, Sutton AJ, Lambert PC. What to add to nothing? Use and avoidance of continuity corrections in meta-analysis of sparse data. Stat Med 2004;23:1351-1375.
Clopper CJ, Pearson ES. The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika 1934;26:404-413.
Higgins JPT, Thompson SG. Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Stat Med 2002;21:1539-1558.
Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.5, section 10.10.2 (Identifying and measuring heterogeneity).
Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.5, section 10.10.4.3 (Prediction intervals in random-effects meta-analysis).
Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Spiegelhalter DJ. A re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis. J R Stat Soc Ser A 2009;172:137-159.
